preamble: Deaspiration of the aspirated alveolar stop [tʰ] to plain [t]. In Ancient Greek it is conditioned by Grassmann's law: when two aspirates occur in successive syllables, the first loses its aspiration, so inherited *tʰ became t before a following aspirate (τίθημι, τριχός, τάφος, ταχύς). In the Nguni languages Xhosa and Zulu, [tʰ] loses its aspiration after a homorganic nasal, most visibly in class 9/10 nouns formed with the prefix iN- (Xhosa thetha 'to speak' > intetho 'speech', Zulu thenga 'to buy' > intengo 'price'); Wikipedia's prenasalisation tables label the rule "Aspiration is lost on obstruents". Zulu realizes the resulting plain stop as an ejective, while Xhosa ejectives are plain tenuis stops except in careful pronunciation or salient positions (Wikipedia, Xhosa language).

examples.note: Grassmann's law: the reduplicating syllable loses aspiration before the aspirated root.
The root keeps its initial aspirate in the nominative θρίξ thríx, where the final aspirate is lost before s.
Compare θάπτειν tháptein 'to bury', where the second aspirate is lost before the t-suffix.
Compare the comparative θάσσων thássōn 'faster', which keeps the initial aspirate.

examples.note: Synchronic alternation. Wikipedia's Xhosa prenasalisation table gives the plural iintetho 'speeches' with [ntʼ]; Wiktionary writes the stop as plain [ⁿt]. The second th, not after a nasal, stays aspirated.
